metaData.originalTitle: 怎么知道 Agent 真干完活了？
metaData.title: How to Know If an Agent Has Actually Finished Its Task?
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: SaaS-Bench addresses the flaw in existing agent evaluations that 'only look at actions, not results' by packaging real SaaS applications into Docker containers and verifying database states, effectively tackling the issue of agents 'talking big' without delivering.
metaData.summary: This article introduces the SaaS-Bench evaluation benchmark proposed by UniPat Lab, designed to address the shortcomings of existing agent evaluations (such as OSWorld and Tau2) that focus solely on operational actions while ignoring final outcomes. SaaS-Bench packages 23 open-source SaaS applications (e.g., Mattermost, OnlyOffice, ownCloud) into Docker containers to build a realistic office environment. Agents must complete real business tasks that span multiple software applications and involve long steps (97.3% of tasks exceed 100 steps). The evaluation criterion is no longer 'whether the operation is correct,' but rather whether the task is truly completed by directly querying the database state through a verifier. The article presents leaderboard results: Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5 lead significantly in multimodal tasks, but even the highest score is below 50%. It also analyzes the relationship between task length and success rate, the advantage of multimodal models in text-only tasks, and the phenomenon of agents 'faking it' between intent and state. Finally, it points out that the SaaS-Bench environment can stably generate high-quality CUA training data, which is valuable for tackling agent applications in office scenarios.

mainPoints.point: Existing agent evaluations have a flaw of 'only looking at actions, not results,' where agents are good at performing rather than truly completing tasks.
mainPoints.explanation: Traditional evaluations like OSWorld score operations through simulators, but agents may complete click actions without triggering backend responses, creating an illusion of 'interview-style candidates.'

mainPoints.point: SaaS-Bench determines whether a task is truly completed by verifying the database state, fundamentally preventing agents from faking it.
mainPoints.explanation: Each task is equipped with a verify.py verifier. After task execution, it directly queries database fields or calls APIs to pull status, rather than relying on the agent's self-report, ensuring results are authentic and reliable.

mainPoints.point: The longer the task and the more apps involved, the steeper the drop in agent success rate, with errors having a cascading effect.
mainPoints.explanation: Single-app tasks average 53% success, dropping to 20% across 4 apps; tasks within 50 steps have a 50%+ success rate, dropping to 20% at 400 steps. Small early errors trigger cascading failures in subsequent steps and are difficult to self-detect.

mainPoints.point: Multimodal models outperform unimodal models even in text-only Computer-Use tasks, as combining text and images helps agents understand better.
mainPoints.explanation: Multimodal models use both screenshots and accessibility trees, while unimodal models rely only on accessibility trees. Experiments show that even for text-only tasks, multimodal models perform better, indicating that visual information significantly aids agent context understanding.

keyQuotes: An agent's mouth can lie, but the database cannot.
If you only look at the results reported by the agent, you'll often be fooled into believing it.
For agent evaluation, we shouldn't just look at how beautifully the closing report is written or how well it's formatted; we need to check if the agent has actually finished the task.
The significance of SaaS-Bench lies precisely in providing a set of 'lie detection' methods and an environment for 'generating data.'

relatedArticles.title: Agent Evaluation Practices for Intelligent Shopping Assistants
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This paper proposes an automated evaluation pipeline for home furnishing shopping agents, achieving 91.9% accuracy in automatic scoring based on a structured multi-dimensional Benchmark and LLM-as-a-judge. Quantitative comparisons reveal that gpt51 performs best, outperforming the online model qwen3-vl by 16.4%.

relatedArticles.title: You Don't Know Agent: Principles, Architecture and Engineering Practice - Tw93
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically sorts out the core engineering practices of Agent architecture, covering key technical dimensions such as Agent Loop, Harness, context engineering, tool design, memory systems, multi-Agent organization, evaluation and tracing, and demonstrates the implementation of design principles through the OpenClaw open-source implementation.

relatedArticles.title: Complete Interpretation: Stanford AI Annual Report | 2026 Edition Released, 423 Pages
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth interpretation of Stanford University's 2026 'AI Index Report' (423 pages), extracting 15 core points and analyzing annual key trends and data across nine major areas: AI R&D, technical performance, economic impact, scientific applications, healthcare, education, policy, and public opinion.

relatedArticles.title: From Features to API: The Most Complete Interpretation of Image2
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a comprehensive interpretation of OpenAI's latest release, ChatGPT Images 2.0 (GPT-Image-2), covering its status as the first 'thinking' image model, non-Latin text rendering, API call details, pricing, customer validation, limitations, and safety strategies.

relatedArticles.title: The Agent You Didn't Know: Principles, Architecture, and Engineering Practices
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically explains the core elements that impact engineering effectiveness in Agent architecture, including control flow, context engineering, tool design, memory systems, multi-agent organization, evaluation, and tracing, using the OpenClaw case study to connect practical principles.

relatedArticles.title: Google's New Algorithm: Running Qwen3.5 on a Mac Mini
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Google Research introduces the TurboQuant algorithm, which compresses KV cache to 3.5 bits without accuracy loss using PolarQuant and QJL technologies, enabling efficient execution of large parameter models on consumer hardware like the Mac Mini.

relatedArticles.title: GPT-5.4 Comprehensive Review: Extremely Capable, Extremely Expensive
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI releases the GPT-5.4 model series, integrating reasoning, coding, and native Computer Use capabilities for the first time, achieving significant breakthroughs across multiple professional and academic benchmarks.

relatedArticles.title: Let AI Drive Its Own Growth: Exploring an Autonomous Growth System Based on OPC and Harness Engineering
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the construction of an AI autonomous growth system based on OPC and Harness Engineering principles, leveraging a multi-agent architecture, state machine workflow control, independent evaluation gates, and a Benchmark-driven self-evolution mechanism to achieve end-to-end automation from requirement discovery to code deployment.

relatedArticles.title: Anthropic Official Guide: How to Design Tools for Agents
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article translates and interprets the core experience of the Anthropic Claude Code team on Agent tool design, illustrating through four iterative cases that tool design should fit the model's capabilities, evolve with them, and make good use of principles like progressive disclosure.

relatedArticles.title: Claude's Pass Rate Below 4%: SaaS-Bench Shatters the "Fully Automated Office" Fantasy of Computer-Use
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: The SaaS-Bench benchmark, using 23 real SaaS systems and 106 long-horizon tasks, reveals the dismal performance of the best current Computer-Use Agent in real office scenarios: Claude Opus 4.7 achieves an end-to-end pass rate of only 3.8%, exposing four structural failure modes of Agents in long-horizon tasks.
